title: Typical atrial flutter
summary: A wavefront circles the tricuspid annulus about 300 times a minute; the AV node passes every second wave.

events.label: Circuit
events.caption: A single wavefront circles the tricuspid annulus counter-clockwise: a macro-reentrant circuit. The circuit is drawn schematically.
events.ecg: The flutter waves form a continuous sawtooth with no flat baseline between them.

events.label: Cavotricuspid isthmus
events.caption: The wavefront crosses the cavotricuspid isthmus, a narrow strip of right atrium between the tricuspid annulus and the inferior vena cava. Conduction is slow here, and this strip is the usual ablation target.
events.ecg: Typical flutter gives negative sawtooth waves in the inferior leads, with an atrial rate near 300 per minute.

events.label: AV node
events.caption: Each wave reaches the AV node, but the node has a long refractory period and cannot conduct every one.
events.ecg: Flutter waves continue; the QRS follows only some of them.

events.label: Conducted beat
events.caption: A conducted impulse activates the ventricles through the normal system, so the QRS is narrow.
events.ecg: A narrow QRS superimposed on the flutter waves.

events.label: Blocked wave
events.caption: The next flutter wave arrives while the AV node is still refractory, and it is blocked. The result is 2:1 conduction: a ventricular rate of about 150.
events.ecg: A flutter wave with no QRS after it. The ventricular rhythm is regular at half the atrial rate.

teaching_points: Typical flutter is a macro-reentrant circuit around the tricuspid annulus, rate about 300 per minute, with sawtooth waves most visible in leads II, III and aVF.
The AV node limits how many impulses reach the ventricles: 2:1 is common (ventricular rate about 150); 4:1 and variable block also occur.
The cavotricuspid isthmus is the critical slow strip and the usual ablation target.
